prize_parts.citation: For showing how differences in productivity across firms, and selection into exporting and foreign investment, shape patterns of trade and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework moved trade theory from industries and countries to firms. It explains who exports, why trade reallocates resources toward more productive firms, and how exporting and foreign direct investment relate to productivity. The model is simple enough to be a standard teaching and quantitative tool. It has also been tested against firm-level microdata for more than twenty years, and it spread into macroeconomics, growth, industrial organisation and firm dynamics. Attribution is relatively clean: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model, and Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple on exports versus FDI and across a long body of trade theory, is the natural co-credit. The two-name set is also easy to defend against the three-name cap. I reconsidered B009 after the openings. It has the broadest support, and I still rank it highly. But I judge it a combination of two strands (technology and tasks, and the trade shock) whose credit is harder to put in one citation, and its overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes is a real concern.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and priority. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and Hopenhayn in the firm-dynamics literature, have strong claims to adjacent ideas and are not on this ballot line. The prize would therefore credit a narrower slice of a larger intellectual movement. Krugman's 2008 prize already recognised new trade theory, and Helpman's separate candidacy (B049) splits his credit. The welfare gains from selection are also smaller than first suggested in some quantitative treatments. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are left out by choice.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B014 second and stresses that trade has not been recognised since Krugman in 2008. He also flags that Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare cast doubt on how large the welfare gains from firm heterogeneity really are, and he notes Bernard, Eaton and Kortum as adjacent claimants.
responses.response: I take the welfare point seriously and think it qualifies the citation rather than defeating the case. Under common restrictions, the aggregate gains can be summarised by a few statistics regardless of whether firms are heterogeneous. But that result has been refined, since the margins of adjustment still matter under other productivity distributions and for distributional and reallocation effects. The lasting contribution is therefore the change in what trade economists model and measure, not the size of a headline welfare number. The citation should be worded around selection and reallocation, not around large aggregate gains. I agree that field balance is a weak argument by itself. The gap since 2008 is not merit, and I do not rest the case on it.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B014 third and flags that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have strong priority claims not credited on this ballot line. She adds that Helpman may be seen as the stronger candidate through B049, which creates an allocation tension.
responses.response: I agree the priority issue is the main weakness, and I cannot dismiss it. My view is that Melitz's model is distinct from the Bernard-Eaton-Kortum line. It supplies tractable selection with fixed costs and a clean link to export participation and reallocation, and the empirical exporter-premium evidence motivated it rather than substituting for it. The committee can word the citation around the theoretical framework with selection into exporting and FDI to reflect that. On B049, the split in Helpman's candidacy is an argument for a citation that rests on the heterogeneous-firm work. It is not an argument that his credit here is weaker, because the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple contribution stands on its own.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B009 first as one of the most compelling cases on the list. He sees Katz as the long-run anchor, Autor and Hanson as central, and Dorn as a close co-author left out by the cap. He also notes that the overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes affects how the citation is framed.
responses.response: I agree B009 is very strong and I keep it as my first alternative. My hesitation is the framing you identify. A citation covering both the task and skill-premium strand (Katz, Autor) and the trade-shock strand (Autor, Hanson, with Dorn) is really two discoveries, and the three-name cap forces an uncomfortable choice that excludes Dorn. The overlap with Goldin and Acemoglu also weakens the technology strand's marginal novelty. If the committee prefers B009, I would want a citation that is tight and states the shared object, labour-market adjustment to technology and trade. I would not simply defer to the first-place count, since it is not evidence of scientific merit.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first but proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He centres the discovery on the China shock and treats Katz's wage-inequality work as a parallel contribution whose credit boundary is contestable.
responses.response: This is a useful disagreement. If the citation is the China shock alone, Autor, Dorn and Hanson is the most accurate set, and dropping Katz is defensible. If the citation includes the technology and wage-structure strand, then Katz is indispensable through the Katz-Murphy and Autor-Katz-Kearney work. The two proposals do not yield one coherent prize unless the committee decides first which discovery it is crediting. That open question is one reason I do not prefer B009 as the lead candidate, even though I rate it highly. B014 does not have this problem, because the credited discovery is a single framework.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation resting on Melitz and Helpman without Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, given the priority claims.
How much weight Krugman's 2008 prize and Helpman's separate B049 candidacy should carry against the case here.
Whether quantitative-trade results that limit the aggregate gains from selection reduce the prize-level importance of the framework, or only the size of the claimed welfare effect.
For B009, whether the technology and trade strands are one discovery, and how to treat Dorn and Katz under the three-name cap.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile documents a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited in B031, an alternative I ranked second in my opening. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it, and I keep B031 as an alternative only. Per Krusell is a frequent co-author and John Hassler a co-author; both are IIES colleagues and neither is credited on B014 or B009. No connection to Melitz, Helpman, Redding, Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from the supplied profile.
